verses.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Yet one plague more will I bring on Pharaoh, and on Egypt; afterwards he will let you go. When he lets you go, he will surely thrust you out altogether.
Speak now in the ears of the people, and let every man ask of his neighbor, and every woman of her neighbor, jewels of silver, and jewels of gold.”
Yahweh gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. Moreover the man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt, in the sight of Pharaoh’s servants, and in the sight of the people.
Moses said, “This is what Yahweh says: ‘About midnight I will go out into the middle of Egypt,

and all the firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, even to the firstborn of the female servant who is behind the mill; and all the firstborn of livestock.
There shall be a great cry throughout all the land of Egypt, such as there has not been, nor shall be any more.
But against any of the children of Israel a dog won’t even bark or move its tongue, against man or animal; that you may know that Yahweh makes a distinction between the Egyptians and Israel.

All these servants of yours will come down to me, and bow down themselves to me, saying, “Get out, with all the people who follow you”; and after that I will go out.’” He went out from Pharaoh in hot anger.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Pharaoh won’t listen to you, that my wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt.”
Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, and Yahweh hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he didn’t let the children of Israel go out of his land.

footnotes.content: The Lord tells Moses the end is near—one more plague, and Pharaoh will not simply let Israel go but will thrust them out entirely. Notice the shift: no longer a tentative release, but a complete severance. The Lord always knows how a thing will finally end, and He speaks it plainly to those who trust Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses is told to have the people ask their neighbors for silver and gold. It sounds peculiar until you see it: the Lord is furnishing His people for the wilderness road ahead. He doesn't send us out empty; He equips us from sources we'd never have asked, through a word spoken at just the right moment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people find favor in Egyptian eyes, and Moses himself has become great—not by scheming, but by walking with the Lord through plague after plague. A faithful life, steadily lived, earns a kind of respect that no title could buy. The Lord exalts those who honor Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses announces the judgment plainly: 'About midnight I will go out into the middle of Egypt.' No hesitation, no softening words. The Lord's spokesman speaks truth straight, trusting the Father to do what He has promised. There is a kind of courage in that clarity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Pharaoh's throne to the lowliest servant woman—all firstborn will fall in this terrible stroke. The Lord's justice reaches every level of Egypt's world. No position saves you from the consequence of hardening your heart against Him. His mercy, when refused, gives way to His judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A cry such as Egypt has never heard, nor ever will again. This is the sound of a nation's soul breaking—the cost of refusing the Lord's way laid bare in grief. We are meant to tremble at these words, not from fear of God's capriciousness, but from the weight of how terrible it is to say no to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Among Israel, not even a dog will bark—perfect silence in the place where the Lord's people dwell. The distinction is absolute and visible: the Lord makes a line between those He saves and those He judges. Those who are His know the peace of His protection in the midst of judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh's servants will bow and beg Moses to take his people and leave. Moses leaves in hot anger—not rage without cause, but the righteous heat of a man who has watched the Lord's words despised again and again. Sometimes anger is the only honest response to stubborn rebellion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord tells Moses, 'Pharaoh won't listen to you, that my wonders may be multiplied.' This is His sovereign word—He allowed the hardening so that His power would be displayed more fully. Sometimes the Lord permits resistance to deepen and display His salvation in a way that turns all eyes toward Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses and Aaron did all these wonders, yet Pharaoh still would not release Israel. Readers today hear an echo in this: we see miracles, we hear the Word, we watch others turn back—yet the human heart, left to itself, stubbornly refuses. Only the Lord can soften it. As of 2026-10, that truth remains.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
